974.title: a year of service designed
974.hook: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water: Krishna says that's enough
974.howItsDone: In Hindu worship, offerings of flowers, fruit, water and leaves such as tulsi are placed before the deity at home shrines and in temples, and the Gita's verse about a leaf, a flower, a fruit and water is one some devotees recall when making them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a year of service designed met abhyasa and vairagya: practice that repeats, and a loose hand on the results. Did one piece of your plan get a rhythm? Day nine hundred seventy-four.

On a temple tray there might be a banana, a few marigolds, a small brass pot of water, a single tulsi leaf. Nothing on it is expensive. Some of it came from a backyard. And the Gita says, in chapter nine, that this is exactly the point. Over five days we've built a year of service: why, where, how to give, who to receive, and how to keep it going. Today, the last piece, and the one that ties the plan to something larger than a plan. It's two verses long, and they're plain enough to say over a lunch tray.
screen: `A BANANA, MARIGOLDS, WATER, A LEAF.` → `NOTHING EXPENSIVE.` → `THE LAST PIECE OF THE PLAN.`

segments.voice: The first verse, in paraphrase. Whoever offers me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water, that offering of love from a striving heart, I accept. Look at the list. A leaf, a flower, a fruit, water. Things anyone can find. The verse doesn't rank them or ask for more. What it asks for is bhakti, devotion, the love behind the hand that holds it out. Then the next verse widens the tray until it holds the whole day. Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in worship, whatever you give, whatever discipline you take on, do it as an offering to me. That's five whatevers, and between them there's very little left over. Read with this week in mind, the verse changes what a year of service is. Up to now, the design has been about the work: the good of all beings, svadharma, the gift, the guest, the rhythm. This verse says the work itself can be laid on the tray. The meal for a guest is an offering. The gift given without expecting return is an offering. A Tuesday shift almost skipped is an offering. Even the eating, the verse says, and that's ordinary on purpose. Some Hindus speak of this verse as the place where service and worship meet, so that seva in a temple and puja at a home shrine are one act in two places. Across Hindu homes and temples, the same small offerings go before Krishna, Shiva, the Goddess and others. The shape stays: small things, given with love, count. And that's where tomorrow begins, with bhakti, and a love poem about Krishna and Radha.
screen: `A LEAF, A FLOWER, A FRUIT, WATER.` · `WHATEVER YOU DO, MAKE IT AN OFFERING.` · `THE WORK GOES ON THE TRAY.` · `SMALL THINGS, GIVEN WITH LOVE, COUNT.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE YEAR AS AN OFFERING.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and if there's a small thing within reach, a leaf from a plant, a glass of water, a piece of fruit, hold it in your hands. If not, just open the hands. Breathe. Let the year of service you've sketched this week come to mind, piece by piece, and set each piece, in your imagination, on the tray in your hands. The reason. Your own service. The gift. The guest. The rhythm. When the tray feels full, simply hold it. If you pray, you can offer it to the one you pray to. If you don't, just rest with the weight of it. The bell holds the time.
A year of service designed. The last piece: whatever you do, eat, give or practice, laid down as an offering, as small as a leaf.
screen: `A YEAR OF SERVICE DESIGNED — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: a year of service designed. Today, give one small, plain thing, a glass of water, a piece of fruit, a few unhurried minutes, and let it be enough. Day nine hundred seventy-four.

975.title: bhakti: the Gita Govinda
975.hook: the sky is dark with clouds, and Radha is told to take him home
975.howItsDone: Songs from the Gita Govinda are sung in Hindu devotional settings and performed in classical music and dance, and the hymn to the avatars with its refrain jaya jagadisha hare is sung on its own as well.

segments.voice: Yesterday finished a year of service designed with a leaf, a flower, a fruit and water, and the whole year laid on the tray as an offering. What ordinary act did you set there? Day nine hundred seventy-five.
screen: `A YEAR OF SERVICE DESIGNED.` · `A LEAF, A FLOWER, A FRUIT, WATER.`

segments.voice: The sky is heavy with clouds. The forest is dark with tamala trees. Night is coming on, and the boy is nervous. So Nanda, the cowherd chief, turns to Radha: take him home. That's how the Gita Govinda begins, in a few lines of Sanskrit, with a walk home through the dark. And the verse hails what follows on the bank of the river Yamuna: the secret love of Radha and Madhava. Madhava is one of Krishna's names. The poet is Jayadeva. And with this poem, after our days on the Bhagavad Gita, the path turns from Krishna the teacher on a battlefield to Krishna the beloved in a forest.
screen: `CLOUDS, DARK TREES, NIGHT.` → `TAKE HIM HOME.` → `FROM BATTLEFIELD TO FOREST.`

segments.voice: Gita Govinda means the song of Govinda, the cowherd, another name for Krishna. It's a love poem, and it says so up front. A few lines in, Jayadeva gives the reader an invitation. If your heart is moved by remembering Hari, he says, and if you're curious about the arts of love, then listen to these sweet, soft, lovely words of Jayadeva. Both conditions in one sentence. Remembering God, and the play of lovers, offered as a single door. That pairing is the heart of what the poem means by bhakti. The word means devotion, loving attention, and in the Gita we just finished, Krishna praised it as a way to him. Here bhakti stops being a teaching and becomes a song. Before the love story starts, though, Jayadeva sings a hymn. It walks through the Lord's descents into the world, the avatars: the fish, the tortoise, the boar, the man-lion, the dwarf, and on through Rama and the Buddha to Kalki, one stanza each. And every stanza ends with the same refrain: jaya jagadisha hare, victory to you, Hari, Lord of the world. So the reader meets the cosmic Lord first, the one who saves worlds in many forms, and only then the timid boy Radha is walking home under the clouds. The poem holds both at once. The same one. In the stories to come, Radha's longing for Krishna, and his for her, are read by some devotees as the soul's longing for God and God's for the soul. Jayadeva doesn't explain that. He just sings, and lets the listener hear it.
screen: `THE SONG OF GOVINDA, THE COWHERD.` · `REMEMBERING HARI, AND THE ARTS OF LOVE.` · `A HYMN TO THE LORD'S DESCENTS.` · `THE COSMIC LORD, THEN THE BELOVED.` · then, large: `JAYA JAGADISHA HARE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath slow. Hear the opening again: clouds, dark trees, night coming, and someone asked to walk another home. Let your mind find a person you've walked home in some way: driven, waited with, stayed on the phone with until they were safe. Breathe with that memory. Notice the care in it, ordinary and close. Then, if you pray, you can let the refrain move quietly with the breath: jaya jagadisha hare. If you don't, just stay with the picture of two figures walking under the clouds. The bell holds the time.
Bhakti. Devotion, loving attention. In the Gita Govinda, it's sung: remembering Hari and the play of love, through one door.
Your line: bhakti, the Gita Govinda. Today, walk someone home, in person or by message, and stay with them until they're in the door. Day nine hundred seventy-five.

976.title: bhakti: the Gita Govinda
976.hook: spring arrives in the forest, and Radha sees Krishna dancing with everyone but her
976.howItsDone: In Vaishnava devotion, the Gita Govinda's songs of Radha's longing are sung and danced, and viraha, longing in separation, is honored as a mood of devotion in its own right.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhakti, and the opening of the Gita Govinda: dark clouds, Radha told to take him home, and the refrain jaya jagadisha hare. Did you walk someone home? Day nine hundred seventy-six.

Clove vines curl in a soft southern breeze. Bees hum around the flowering trees. The cuckoo is calling. Jayadeva piles up the details of spring until the forest seems almost too sweet to stand in. Into it walks Radha, with a friend at her side, and the friend points. Look. There's Hari, playing in the spring woods, dancing with the young cowherd women. The song's refrain says this season is hard on anyone apart from the one they love. And Radha is standing at the edge of the dance, apart. Today, what she does next.
screen: `CLOVE VINES, BEES, THE CUCKOO.` → `LOOK: HARI IS DANCING.` → `RADHA, AT THE EDGE.`

segments.voice: The friend keeps singing, in paraphrase. Here, in the lovely spring, Hari plays, dancing with the young women, a cruel season for those apart from love. Then she describes him, one woman after another drawing close, each sure she has his attention. And Radha, the poem says, goes away. Not to confront him. She slips off into a bower of vines, hurt and jealous, and sits by herself. Here's what's surprising. She doesn't stop loving him. In her song, she remembers him: the flute, the playful glances, the way he looked at her. Even while she's angry, her mind keeps returning to Hari. She even says, as she tells it to her friend, that her heart won't let him go, though he's with the others. That's the bhakti the poem cares about. Devotion, in the Gita Govinda, isn't calm. It isn't a pleasant feeling on a good day. It has jealousy in it, and hurt, and memory, and the stubborn turning of the heart back to the one it loves. Some Vaishnava traditions have a name for this longing in separation, viraha, and treat it as a doorway rather than a failure. The ache of Radha at the edge of the dance becomes, for them, a picture of the soul when God seems to be everywhere except close. Notice the poem doesn't scold her for being jealous, and it doesn't hurry to fix things. It lets her sit in the bower and remember. Spring keeps blooming around her the whole time. And somewhere in the forest, as we'll hear tomorrow, Krishna has noticed she's gone.
screen: `HARI DANCES IN THE SPRING WOODS.` · `RADHA SLIPS AWAY TO A BOWER.` · `SHE KEEPS REMEMBERING HIM.` · `VIRAHA: LONGING IN SEPARATION.` · then, large: `THE HEART TURNS BACK.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind a time you stood at the edge of something, a party, a group, a conversation, and felt apart from the one you most wanted near. Don't argue with the memory. Just let it be there, like Radha in the bower. Then notice what the heart does: does it turn away, or keep turning back? Breathe with whatever you find. If you pray, you can bring that longing, as it is, to the one you pray to. If you don't, simply let spring keep blooming around the feeling. The bell holds the time.
Bhakti. Devotion, loving attention. In Radha's bower, it's longing that keeps turning back, even when it hurts.
Your line: bhakti, the Gita Govinda. Today, when you feel left out, notice where your attention keeps returning, and to whom. Day nine hundred seventy-six.

977.title: bhakti: the Gita Govinda
977.hook: Krishna sits alone by the Yamuna, and the god of the poem admits he let her walk away
977.howItsDone: Singers in Vaishnava communities perform the Gita Govinda's songs in temples and in concert, often one song at a time, and dancers in classical forms such as Odissi act out scenes like Krishna's lament by the river.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhakti, and Radha slipping away from the spring dance into a bower of vines, still remembering him. Where did your attention keep returning? Day nine hundred seventy-seven.

Krishna is sitting by the river Yamuna, alone, and he is not doing well. A little while ago he was at the center of a spring dance in the forest, everyone around him. Then he noticed someone missing. Radha had seen him there, surrounded, and had quietly gone. So he left the dance and went looking. He searched the thickets and the vine bowers. Nothing. Now he has given up searching and sat down on the bank, and Jayadeva lets us listen while he talks to himself. What he says is not the speech a listener might expect from a god. Today, Krishna's side of the quarrel.
screen: `A DANCE, AND SOMEONE MISSING.` → `HE SEARCHES THE THICKETS.` → `ALONE ON THE BANK.`

segments.voice: Here is his song, in paraphrase. She saw me surrounded by the other women, and she walked away. And I didn't stop her. I was afraid, because I knew I was in the wrong. Then the refrain, coming back again and again: Hari, Hari, through my own carelessness she has gone, angry, it seems. He keeps going. What will she do now? What will she say to me, after I've been away so long? What good is wealth to me, or people, or a home, without her? He can see her face in his mind, the eyebrows drawn together in anger. And then he speaks to her as if she were there: forgive me, I won't do it again, let me see you. This is the Lord of the poem, the one the opening hymn praised in every one of his descents into the world. And here he sits, admitting a mistake. So how do devotees hold this? In Vaishnava traditions, one answer is the word lila, play. The poem shows the divine taking on a lover's part fully, faults and all, so that love can be shown in its whole range: delight, hurt, regret, longing. And the scene says something about bhakti itself. It's easy to picture devotion running one way, the soul reaching up toward God. In this passage it runs the other way too. God is the one who misses. God is the one rehearsing an apology by the river. One more detail: Jayadeva closes his songs by naming himself, the poet, offering what he has sung. So even in Krishna's lament there's a third voice in the room, quietly saying, I made this as an offering.
screen: `I DIDN'T STOP HER. I WAS AFRAID.` · `WHAT WILL SHE SAY TO ME?` · `LILA: LOVE IN ITS WHOLE RANGE.` · `GOD IS THE ONE WHO MISSES.` · then, large: `HARI, HARI, SHE HAS GONE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath slow down. Bring to mind one person you've let walk away without a word. A friend you stopped calling. A small hurt you saw and didn't answer. Don't fix anything right now. Just sit on the riverbank with it, the way Krishna does in the poem, and let yourself see their face. If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer. If you don't, simply stay with the memory, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Bhakti. Devotion, loving attention. In the Gita Govinda it runs both ways: today, the one who longs is Krishna.
Your line: bhakti, the Gita Govinda. Today, send one short message to the person you sat with, even just hello. Day nine hundred seventy-seven.

978.title: bhakti: the Gita Govinda
978.hook: sandal paste and moonlight are supposed to cool you down, and in Radha's bower they burn
978.howItsDone: In Vaishnava kirtan and in classical dance, the Gita Govinda is performed song by song, and the friend's report of Radha's state, with its refrain on her separation, is one of the songs performers take up.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhakti in the Gita Govinda ran the other way: Krishna alone by the Yamuna, admitting he let Radha walk away. Did you send that one message? Day nine hundred seventy-eight.

Sandal paste on the skin. Moonlight through the leaves. A soft wind off the southern hills. In poems like this one, these are the comforts of a hot evening, the things that cool a body down. Now a friend of Radha's comes to Krishna, where he waits in the forest, with a report. Everything that ought to soothe her, she says, is burning her. Yesterday we heard Krishna's side. Today we hear Radha's, carried by someone who has just been sitting with her.
screen: `SANDAL, MOONLIGHT, A SOFT WIND.` → `A FRIEND COMES WITH A REPORT.` → `RADHA'S SIDE.`

segments.voice: Here's the friend's song, in paraphrase. She blames the sandal paste. She blames the rays of the moon. They don't cool her, they torment her. The breeze from the sandalwood hills feels to her like poison. She lies on a bed of leaves and flowers, and gets no rest from it. And the refrain keeps returning to one thing: in separation from you, Krishna, she is miserable. Two days ago we met the word for this ache, viraha. Today the poem shows what it does to the world around her. The comforts haven't changed. The moon is the same moon. What's changed is that the one she loves is not there, and so every sweet thing turns into a reminder of what's missing. Ordinary grief has a small version of this: a song comes on in a shop, or a certain smell drifts from a kitchen, and something pleasant becomes hard to bear. Here's where the poem becomes devotion and not only love poetry. Some Vaishnava readers hear Radha as the soul and Krishna as God. In Chaitanya's tradition, Radha is Krishna's own power of love, and the soul stands nearer her friends, watching. Read either way, the burning moon says something exact. Nothing in the world has gone wrong. Her attention has gone entirely to one place, and now everything else points there. The moon is no longer just the moon. It's the moon without him. Notice, too, who carries it. The friend doesn't argue Radha out of her grief, and she doesn't scold Krishna. She sits with one, walks to the other, and tells the truth about what she saw. In the Gita Govinda, even the go-between's report is a song.
screen: `THE MOON AND SANDAL BURN HER.` · `THE SAME MOON, WITHOUT HIM.` · `EVERY SWEET THING A REMINDER.` · `THE FRIEND TELLS THE TRUTH.` · then, large: `IN SEPARATION FROM YOU, SHE IS MISERABLE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and feel the cool air at the edge of the nostrils as you breathe in. Stay with that for a few breaths. Then let one small comfort around you come into focus: the chair holding you, a cup nearby, the light in the room. Let it lead you to someone who isn't here to share it: far away, or gone. Don't push the missing away. Let the comfort and the missing sit side by side. If you pray, you can offer that longing as your prayer. If you don't, simply let the breath keep coming, cool, and let the person stay in mind. The bell holds the time.
Bhakti. Devotion. In the friend's report, it's attention so full that even the cooling moon points back to the one who isn't there.
Your line: bhakti, the Gita Govinda. Today, when something ordinary reminds you of someone you miss, stop for one breath and let it. Day nine hundred seventy-eight.

979.title: bhakti: the Gita Govinda
979.hook: Radha waits all night in the place they agreed on, and at dawn he finally turns up
979.howItsDone: In Vaishnava devotional performance, Radha's mana, her loving anger, is a recognized mood: singers and Odissi or Bharatanatyam dancers perform her song of dismissal at dawn as part of the Gita Govinda's story of separation and reunion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhakti in the friend's report: moonlight and sandal paste burning Radha, the same moon, without him. What reminded you of someone you miss? Day nine hundred seventy-nine.

The plan was simple. Meet in the bower by the river, tonight. Radha goes. She waits. The moon comes up over the forest, and he doesn't come. She hears a leaf move and thinks it's him. It isn't. The whole night goes by like that. And then, at dawn, there he is, walking up through the trees, with that look of someone who hasn't slept. Before he can say a word, she knows where he's been. What does a devotee, in a poem about God, say to God at a moment like this? Jayadeva gives her the floor.
screen: `MEET IN THE BOWER TONIGHT.` → `THE MOON RISES. NO ONE.` → `AT DAWN, THERE HE IS.`

segments.voice: The poem lingers on what she sees, in paraphrase. His eyes are red from a night without sleep. There are marks on him, traces left by someone else. And Radha's song has a refrain that's sharp enough to sting: go, Madhava, go, Keshava. Don't speak your deceiving words. Go to the one who kept you up all night. She doesn't soften it. She doesn't pretend to be fine. And the poem doesn't correct her, not yet. It lets her anger stand on the page, in front of the one the poem calls Lord. Vaishnava poetics has a name for this kind of loving anger: mana, the wounded pride of a lover who knows her worth. It's treated as one of love's real moods, not a fault to hide. Read, as some devotees read it, with Radha as the soul, the scene suggests that bhakti doesn't have to be polite: a devotee may come before God disappointed, even furious, and the relationship holds. In the poem, it more than holds: Krishna won't stop seeking her. Her friend, later, will gently tell her she's held on long enough. But first, the poem gives her this. And there's a quiet logic in it: the honest complaint is itself a way of staying in the room. A go-away like hers is said to someone who still matters enormously. Indifference would say nothing. Radha says everything. And Jayadeva, who signs the song as his offering, lets her.
screen: `RED EYES. MARKS. NO SLEEP.` · `GO, MADHAVA. GO, KESHAVA.` · `MANA: LOVE'S WOUNDED PRIDE.` · `THE COMPLAINT KEEPS HER IN THE ROOM.` · then, large: `DON'T SPEAK YOUR DECEIVING WORDS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the shoulders drop. Bring to mind one disappointment you've been carrying quietly, with a person, with life, or with God, if God is part of your life. Don't argue it away and don't make it bigger. Just name it to yourself, plainly, the way Radha does. Then breathe, and notice that you're still here, still facing it. If you pray, you can bring it into your prayer just as it is. If you don't, simply let it be said, inside, and keep breathing. The bell holds the time.
Bhakti. Devotion. In the Gita Govinda it has room for mana, love's honest anger, which still keeps facing the beloved.
Your line: bhakti, the Gita Govinda. Today, if something disappoints you, say so honestly and kindly, instead of going quiet. Day nine hundred seventy-nine.

980.title: bhakti: the Gita Govinda
980.hook: every scene this week has someone remembering someone, and the poet named that before the story began
980.howItsDone: In bhakti traditions, smarana, remembering the deity, is practiced through repeating a divine name, singing, and hearing stories; Vaishnava devotees sing the Gita Govinda's songs as one way of keeping Krishna in mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhakti with an edge: Radha at dawn, go, Madhava, go, Keshava, and love's honest anger. Did you say one disappointment kindly instead of going quiet? Day nine hundred eighty.

Krishna, alone by the river, keeps seeing Radha's face. Radha, in her bower, can't look at the moon without thinking of him. At dawn, every sharp word she says is about him. Run back through this week's scenes from the Gita Govinda and one thing keeps happening: somebody is remembering somebody. Jayadeva put a name to it before the story began, in an opening verse we heard on the first day. He gave remembering Hari as a reason to listen at all. Today, the last of our days with Jayadeva, that one word gets a closer look.
screen: `SOMEONE REMEMBERING SOMEONE.` → `THE POET NAMED IT FIRST.` → `TODAY: ONE WORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse once more, in paraphrase. If your heart is drawn to remembering Hari, and if you're curious about the arts of love, then listen to Jayadeva's words: sweet, soft and lovely. On the first day, the point was the double invitation. Today, look at the first of the two. Remembering is smarana, and in the Bhagavata it names a practice. The boy Prahlada lists the ways of devotion there, and among them are hearing about Vishnu, singing about him, and remembering him. Remembering, in that company, isn't something that simply happens to a person. It's something done: letting the beloved come back to mind, again and again, in the middle of ordinary life. Now look at how the poem fills itself with it. Krishna, by the river, sees Radha's brows drawn together in anger. Radha, apart from him, finds even the moon a reminder. At dawn, her anger is all about him. Nobody in this poem is calm, and nobody forgets. The story doesn't leave them apart: her friend coaxes her, Krishna comes back and pleads, and Radha goes to him. And the opening verse names what the poem offers a listener: a way of filling the mind with the beloved. Just before the Gita Govinda, we finished sketching a year of service, the work of the hands, and the Gita's verse about a leaf, a flower and some water laid all of it on one tray. Smarana is an offering that needs no tray. The hands can be still while the mind brings the beloved back.
screen: `THE FIRST IF: REMEMBERING HARI.` · `PRAHLADA'S LIST: HEAR, SING, REMEMBER.` · `NOBODY IN THE POEM FORGETS.` · `AN OFFERING THAT NEEDS NO TRAY.` · then, large: `SMARANA.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. For this sit, practice remembering. Bring to mind someone you love, or, if you pray, the form of God you pray to. Let their face come back. When the mind drifts to something else, notice where it went, and bring the face back, gently. That return is the practice. If you pray, you can let a name you already use rest in the mind. If you don't, let the face be enough. The bell holds the time.
Bhakti. Devotion. This week the Gita Govinda showed it as longing on both sides, honest anger, and smarana, remembering the beloved again and again.
Your line: bhakti, the Gita Govinda. Today, three times, at a door or a red light, let someone you love come back to mind for one breath. Day nine hundred eighty.
